note_text: The meme's claim is false. The 22nd Amendment limits anyone to being elected president twice, regardless of impeachment. Impeachment without Senate conviction doesn't "nullify" a term or reset eligibility. Trump has been elected twice (2016, 2024) and cannot run again. https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/amendment-22/
search_results:
The meme's core claim—that House impeachment of Trump without Senate conviction nullifies his first term, resetting his eligibility to run for president "2 more times" under the **22nd Amendment**—is **false**.

**The 22nd Amendment** explicitly limits any person to being **elected president no more than twice**, regardless of impeachment, conviction, or term completion status: "No person shall be elected to the office of the President more than twice..."[1][2][3][4]. It contains no provision linking impeachment outcomes to term limits or nullification of prior service[1][2][3].

Impeachment by the House is a non-binding accusation; only **Senate conviction** removes a president from office (per Article II, Section 4), but even then, it does not retroactively erase prior elected terms or alter **22nd Amendment** eligibility, which counts elections served[1][5]. Trump has already been **elected twice** (2016, 2024), barring future elections irrespective of any impeachment proceedings[1][2][5].

No credible source supports the meme's claim; it misinterprets constitutional text without reference to impeachment mechanisms[3][4]. For full **22nd Amendment** text: https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/amendment-22/[3].

note_text: The 24-hour rule is too strict. Food safety authorities say properly cooled rice stored in the fridge is safe for 3-6 days. Cool rice within 2 hours, store in airtight containers below 40°F, and reheat thoroughly. https://www.riceland.com/the-riceland-blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-storing-and-reheating-rice-tips-tricks-from-riceland-foods
search_results:
**The claim that cooked rice must be thrown out after exactly 24 hours is inaccurate and overly simplistic.** Food safety authorities provide varying guidelines based on proper cooling and storage: some recommend up to 24 hours (UK Food Standards Agency[4]), while others state 3-4 days (USDA via Varga Bar[2]) or 4-6 days (Riceland Foods[1]) when refrigerated promptly in shallow airtight containers below 5°C/40°F.

### Key Claims from Video and Fact-Check
| Video Claim | Fact-Check |
|-------------|------------|
| **Throw out rice after 24 hours; toxins from bacteria like Bacillus cereus are heat-resistant and cause sickness even after reheating.** | Partially accurate—*Bacillus cereus* spores in uncooked rice can survive cooking, multiply during slow cooling (5-60°C/"danger zone"), and produce heat-stable toxins causing vomiting/diarrhea (not guaranteed sickness). Risk minimized by cooling quickly (within 2 hours), storing shallowly in fridge. Safe reheating to steaming hot kills live bacteria but not all toxins. No 24-hour mandate: https://www.healthywa.wa.gov.au/Articles/S_T/Safe-cooling-of-cooked-rice[3]; https://www.food.gov.uk/safety-hygiene/home-food-fact-checker[4]. |
| **Rice is "fastest growing mold food"; mold often invisible, causes digestive issues and liver cancer.** | Unsupported—Mold growth possible but not uniquely fast on rice; *B. cereus* is bacterial, not mold. No evidence linking to liver cancer; toxins mainly cause acute food poisoning (fried rice syndrome). Visible mold (as in video) indicates spoilage, but safety based on storage time/temp. No sources confirm "carcinogenic toxins" from rice mold. https://www.healthywa.wa.gov.au/Articles/S_T/Safe-cooling-of-cooked-rice[3]. |
| **Japan passed "Rice Act" in 1921; most Asians never eat leftovers.** | False—No "Rice Act" or 1921 law found banning leftovers. *B. cereus* outbreaks (e.g., 1977 Japan) led to better cooling practices, but leftovers common in Asia with proper handling. No supporting sources. |

**Safe storage consensus:** Cool rice rapidly (spread in shallow <10cm containers, fridge within 2 hours), store airtight at ≤5°C, consume within 1-6 days depending on guidelines, reheat once to >60°C/140°F. Discard if smells off or sat out >2 hours. https://www.riceland.com/the-riceland-blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-storing-and-reheating-rice-tips-tricks-from-riceland-foods[1]; https://vargabar.com/how-long-does-cooked-rice-last-in-the-fridge[2].

note_text: This video misrepresents a real 2017 Estonia incident. Two workers (not one person) rescued the wolf from the shore, then drove it to a vet clinic. There was no cave shelter, personal feeding, or pack tracking them down—the wolf was treated by vets and released. https://www.boredpanda.com/man-rescue-wolf-dog-icy-water/
search_results:
The video depicts a **staged or misrepresented animal rescue**, likely drawing from a real 2017 incident in Estonia where two workers rescued a hypothermic wolf (initially thought to be a dog) from a frozen lake, but omitting key contradictions to the viral claims.[1]

### Core Claims vs. Evidence
- **Claim: A solo person ("I") spotted a wolf under ice, pulled it out alone while in the water, sheltered it in a cave, fed it, and the wolf's pack later tracked them down.**
  - **Contradiction**: The real event involved **two workers** (not one person) who rescued the animal from the lake's edge using a car towel for warming, then immediately drove it to a veterinary clinic run by the Estonian Union for the Protection of Animals (EUPA). No solo cave sheltering, personal feeding, or pack tracking occurred; the wolf was GPS-collared by the National Environmental Agency, treated professionally, and released into the wild.[1] https://www.boredpanda.com/man-rescue-wolf-dog-icy-water/
  - Video signs of staging include edited text overlays, dramatic solo narration/audio ("I got you! Help me!" despite no helpers shown), and a dark canine that matches descriptions of the Estonian wolf but is reframed fictionally.[1][2]

- **Claim: The wolf trusted the rescuer despite starvation, and the pack appeared friendly/waiting.**
  - **Contradiction**: Post-rescue, the workers handed the exhausted, hypothermic wolf directly to EUPA without personal bonding or pack involvement; it was stabilized by vets ("Check his lungs! Stabilizing. He's a fighter" matches clinic audio, but no pack was present or tracked them).[1] Wild wolf packs do not typically "track down" and benignly approach humans in this manner; such narratives mimic debunked viral tropes.[2][3] https://www.crittercarewildlife.org/the-truth-behind-fake-animal-rescue-videos https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2019/nov/20/viral-image/facebook-posts-viral-wolf-pack-image-miscategorize/

### Why It's Likely Fake/Staged
This matches patterns of **fake animal rescue videos**, where real events are altered with scripting, AI elements, or reused footage for emotional virality. The video fails the A.R.C. test: no verifiable rescue org (solo claim vs. EUPA/clinic), unnatural solo-hero drama on real ice rescue, and suspicious emotive elements like "pack waiting."[2] The 2017 Estonia story (not recent) has been recycled in viral clips without crediting the team or accurate outcome.[1]
